The seventh in descent from Seth, being the only son of Methuselah. Noah was the oldest of his several sons ([Gen. 5:25-31](#Gen.5.25); [Luke 3:36](#Luke.3.36)).

The fifth in descent from Cain. He was the first to violate the primeval ordinance of marriage ([Gen. 4:18-24](#Gen.4.18)). His address to his two wives, Adah and Zillah (4:23, 24), is the only extant example of antediluvian poetry. It has been called “Lamech’s sword-song.” He was “rude and ruffianly,” fearing neither God nor man. With him the curtain falls on the race of Cain. We know nothing of his descendants.

Torches. Deborah is called “the wife of Lapidoth” ([Judg. 4:4](#Judg.4.4)). Some have rendered the expression “a woman of a fiery spirit,” under the supposition that Lapidoth is not a proper name, a woman of a torch-like spirit.

The brother of Mary and Martha of Bethany. He was raised from the dead after he had lain four days in the tomb ([John 11:1-44](#John.11.1)). This miracle so excited the wrath of the Jews that they sought to put both Jesus and Lazarus to death.

Weary, the eldest daughter of Laban, and sister of Rachel ([Gen. 29:16](#Gen.29.16)). Jacob took her to wife through a deceit of her father ([Gen. 29:23](#Gen.29.23)). She was “tender-eyed” (17). She bore to Jacob six sons (32-35), also one daughter, Dinah (30:21). She accompanied Jacob into Canaan, and died there before the time of the going down into Egypt ([Gen. 31](#Gen.31)), and was buried in the cave of Machpelah (49:31).

Breast, the name of one of the apostles ([Mark 3:18](#Mark.3.18)), called “Lebbaeus” in [Matt. 10:3](#Matt.10.3), and in [Luke 6:16](#Luke.6.16), “Judas the brother of James;” while John (14:22), probably referring to the same person, speaks of “Judas, not Iscariot.” These different names all designate the same person, viz., Jude or Judas, the author of the epistle.
Dedicated to God, a king whom his mother instructed ([Prov. 31:1-9](#Prov.31.1)). Nothing is certainly known concerning him. The rabbis identified him with Solomon.
Peoples; nations, the last mentioned of the three sons of Dedan, and head of an Arabian tribe ([Gen. 25:3](#Gen.25.3)).

The third son of Jacob by Leah. The origin of the name is found in Leah’s words ([Gen. 29:34](#Gen.29.34)), “This time will my husband be joined [Heb. yillaveh] unto me.” He is mentioned as taking a prominent part in avenging his sister Dinah ([Gen. 34:25-31](#Gen.34.25)). He and his three sons went down with Jacob (46:11) into Egypt, where he died at the age of one hundred and thirty-seven years ([Ex. 6:16](#Exod.6.16)).
The father of Matthat, and son of Simeon, of the ancestors of Christ ([Luke 3:29](#Luke.3.29)).

Not my people, a symbolical name given by God’s command to Hosea’s second son in token of Jehovah’s rejection of his people ([Hos. 1:9](#Hos.1.9), [10](#Hos.1.10)), his treatment of them as a foreign people. This Hebrew word is rendered by “not my people” in ver. 10; 2:23.
Not pitied, the name of the prophet Hosea’s first daughter, a type of Jehovah’s temporary rejection of his people ([Hos. 1:6](#Hos.1.6); [2:23](#Hos.2.23)).
The maternal grandmother of Timothy. She is commended by Paul for her faith ([2 Tim. 1:5](#2Tim.1.5)).

(Heb. goral, a “pebble”), a small stone used in casting lots ([Num. 33:54](#Num.33.54); [Jonah 1:7](#Jonah.1.7)). The lot was always resorted to by the Hebrews with strictest reference to the interposition of God, and as a method of ascertaining the divine will ([Prov. 16:33](#Prov.16.33)), and in serious cases of doubt ([Esther 3:7](#Esth.3.7)). Thus the lot was used at the division of the land of Canaan among the serveral tribes ([Num. 26:55](#Num.26.55); [34:13](#Num.34.13)), at the detection of Achan ([Josh. 7:14](#Josh.7.14), [18](#Josh.7.18)), the election of Saul to be king ([1 Sam. 10:20](#1Sam.10.20), [21](#1Sam.10.21)), the distribution of the priestly offices of the temple service ([1 Chr. 24:3](#1Chr.24.3), [5](#1Chr.24.5), [19](#1Chr.24.19); [Luke 1:9](#Luke.1.9)), and over the two goats at the feast of Atonement ([Lev. 16:8](#Lev.16.8)). Matthias, who was “numbered with the eleven” ([Acts 1:24-26](#Acts.1.24)), was chosen by lot.
Coverer, one of the sons of Seir, the Horite ([Gen. 36:20](#Gen.36.20), [29](#Gen.36.29)).
Brilliant star, a title given to the king of Babylon ([Isa. 14:12](#Isa.14.12)) to denote his glory.

Of Cyrene, a Christian teacher at Antioch ([Acts 13:1](#Acts.13.1)), and Paul’s kinsman ([Rom. 16:21](#Rom.16.21)). His name is Latin, but his birthplace seems to indicate that he was one of the Jews of Cyrene, in North Africa.
The fourth son of Shem ([Gen. 10:22](#Gen.10.22); [1 Chr. 1:17](#1Chr.1.17)), ancestor of the Lydians probably.
Probably the same as Lud (2) (comp. [Gen. 10:13](#Gen.10.13); [1 Chr. 1:11](#1Chr.1.11)). They are associated ([Jer. 46:9](#Jer.46.9)) with African nations as mercenaries of the king of Egypt.

The evangelist, was a Gentile. The date and circumstances of his conversion are unknown. According to his own statement ([Luke 1:2](#Luke.1.2)), he was not an “eye-witness and minister of the word from the beginning.” It is probable that he was a physician in Troas, and was there converted by Paul, to whom he attached himself. He accompanied him to Philippi, but did not there share his imprisonment, nor did he accompany him further after his release in his missionary journey at this time ([Acts 17:1](#Acts.17.1)). On Paul’s third visit to Philippi (20:5, 6) we again meet with Luke, who probably had spent all the intervening time in that city, a period of seven or eight years. …

A woman of Thyatira, a “seller of purple,” who dwelt in Philippi ([Acts 16:14](#Acts.16.14), [15](#Acts.16.15)). She was not a Jewess but a proselyte. The Lord opened her heart as she heard the gospel from the lips of Paul (16:13). She thus became the first in Europe who embraced Christianity. She was a person apparently of considerable wealth, for she could afford to give a home to Paul and his companions.
Tetrarch of Abilene ([Luke 3:1](#Luke.3.1)), on the eastern slope of Anti-Lebanon, near the city of Damascus.
A daughter of Talmai, king of the old native population of Geshur. She became one of David’s wives, and was the mother of Absalom ([2 Sam. 3:3](#2Sam.3.3)).

The daughter of Abishalom (called Absalom, [2 Chr. 11:20-22](#2Chr.11.20)), the third wife of Rehoboam, and mother of Abijam ([1 Kings 15:2](#1Kgs.15.2)). She is called “Michaiah the daughter of Uriel,” who was the husband of Absalom’s daughter Tamar ([2 Chr. 13:2](#2Chr.13.2)). Her son Abijah or Abijam was heir to the throne.
The father of Achish, the king of Gath ([1 Kings 2:39](#1Kgs.2.39)), called also Maoch ([1 Sam. 27:2](#1Sam.27.2)).
The father of Hanan, who was one of David’s body-guard ([1 Chr. 11:43](#1Chr.11.43)).
The father of the priest Zephaniah ([Jer. 21:1](#Jer.21.1); [37:3](#Jer.37.3)).
One of the Levites whom David appointed as porter for the ark ([1 Chr. 15:18](#1Chr.15.18), [20](#1Chr.15.20)).
One of the “captains of hundreds” associated with Jehoiada in restoring king Jehoash to the throne ([2 Chr. 23:1](#2Chr.23.1)).

One who was sent by king Josiah to repair the temple ([2 Chr. 34:8](#2Chr.34.8)). He was governor (Heb. sar, rendered elsewhere in the Authorized Version “prince,” “chief captain,” chief ruler”) of Jerusalem.
Work of Jehovah, one of the priests resident at Jerusalem at the Captivity ([1 Chr. 9:12](#1Chr.9.12)).
Small, a person named in our Lord’s ancestry ([Luke 3:26](#Luke.3.26)).
The head of the twenty-fourth priestly course ([1 Chr. 24:18](#1Chr.24.18)) in David’s reign.

Manasseh’s oldest son ([Josh. 17:1](#Josh.17.1)), or probably his only son (see [1 Chr. 7:14](#1Chr.7.14), [15](#1Chr.7.15); comp. [Num. 26:29-33](#Num.26.29); [Josh. 13:31](#Josh.13.31)). His descendants are referred to under the name of Machirites, being the offspring of Gilead ([Num. 26:29](#Num.26.29)). They settled in land taken from the Amorites ([Num. 32:39](#Num.32.39), [40](#Num.32.40); [Deut. 3:15](#Deut.3.15)) by a special enactment ([Num. 36:1-3](#Num.36.1); [Josh. 17:3](#Josh.17.3), [4](#Josh.17.4)). He is once mentioned as the representative of the tribe of Manasseh east of Jordan ([Judg. 5:14](#Judg.5.14)).

A descendant of the preceding, residing at Lo-debar, where he maintained Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth till he was taken under the care of David ([2 Sam. 9:4](#2Sam.9.4)), and where he afterwards gave shelter to David himself when he was a fugitive (17:27).
Middle land, the third “son” of Japheth ([Gen. 10:2](#Gen.10.2)), the name by which the Medes are known on the Assyrian monuments.

Region of Gog, the second of the “sons” of Japheth ([Gen. 10:2](#Gen.10.2); [1 Chr. 1:5](#1Chr.1.5)). In Ezekiel (38:2; 39:6) it is the name of a nation, probably some Scythian or Tartar tribe descended from Japheth. They are described as skilled horsemen, and expert in the use of the bow. The Latin father Jerome says that this word denotes “Scythian nations, fierce and innumerable, who live beyond the Caucasus and the Lake Maeotis, and near the Caspian Sea, and spread out even onward to India.” Perhaps the name “represents the Assyrian Mat Gugi, or ‘country of Gugu,’ the Gyges of the Greeks” (Sayce’s Races, etc.).
The son of Cainan, of the line of Seth ([Gen. 5:12-17](#Gen.5.12)); called Maleleel ([Luke 3:37](#Luke.3.37)).
The daughter of Jerimoth, who was one of David’s sons. She was one of Rehoboam’s wives ([2 Chr. 11:18](#2Chr.11.18)).
A Kohathite Levite, father of Elkanah ([1 Chr. 6:35](#1Chr.6.35)).
Another Kohathite Levite, of the time of Hezekiah ([2 Chr. 29:12](#2Chr.29.12)).
Visions, a Kohathite Levite, chief of the twenty-third course of musicians ([1 Chr. 25:4](#1Chr.25.4), [30](#1Chr.25.30)).

Plunder speedeth; spoil hasteth, ([Isa. 8:1-3](#Isa.8.1); comp. [Zeph. 1:14](#Zeph.1.14)), a name Isaiah was commanded first to write in large characters on a tablet, and afterwards to give as a symbolical name to a son that was to be born to him ([Isa. 8:1](#Isa.8.1), [3](#Isa.8.3)), as denoting the sudden attack on Damascus and Syria by the Assyrian army.
Disease, one of the five daughters of Zelophehad ([Num. 27:1-11](#Num.27.1)) who had their father’s inheritance, the law of inheritance having been altered in their favour.
Sickly, the elder of Elimelech the Bethlehemite’s two sons by Naomi. He married Ruth and died childless ([Ruth 1:2](#Ruth.1.2), [5](#Ruth.1.5); 4:9, 10), in the land of Moab.
Dance, the father of four sons ([1 Kings 4:31](#1Kgs.4.31)) who were inferior in wisdom only to Solomon.

Messenger or angel, the last of the minor prophets, and the writer of the last book of the Old Testament canon ([Mal. 4:4](#Mal.4.4), [5](#Mal.4.5), [6](#Mal.4.6)). Nothing is known of him beyond what is contained in his book of prophecies. Some have supposed that the name is simply a title descriptive of his character as a messenger of Jehovah, and not a proper name. There is reason, however, to conclude that Malachi was the ordinary name of the prophet.

([2 Sam. 12:30](#2Sam.12.30), Heb., R.V., “their king;” [Jer. 49:1](#Jer.49.1), [3](#Jer.49.3), R.V.; [Zeph. 1:5](#Zeph.1.5)), the national idol of the Ammonites. When Rabbah was taken by David, the crown of this idol was among the spoils. The weight is said to have been “a talent of gold” (above 100 lbs.). The expression probably denotes its value rather than its weight. It was adorned with precious stones.
King of help, one of the four sons of Saul ([1 Chr. 8:33](#1Chr.8.33)). He perished along with his father in the battle of Gilboa ([1 Sam. 31:2](#1Sam.31.2)).
A priest who stood by Ezra when he “read in the book of the law of God” ([Neh. 8:4](#Neh.8.4)).
The head of the fifth division of the priests in the time of David ([1 Chr. 24:9](#1Chr.24.9)).
One of the priests appointed as musicians to celebrate the completion of the walls of Jerusalem ([Neh. 12:42](#Neh.12.42)).

Reigning, the personal servant or slave of the high priest Caiaphas. He is mentioned only by John. Peter cut off his right ear in the garden of Gethsemane ([John 18:10](#John.18.10)). But our Lord cured it with a touch ([Matt. 26:51](#Matt.26.51); [Mark 14:47](#Mark.14.47); [Luke 22:51](#Luke.22.51)). This was the last miracle of bodily cure wrought by our Lord. It is not mentioned by John.
My fulness, a Kohathite Levite, one of the sons of Heman the Levite ([1 Chr. 25:4](#1Chr.25.4)), and chief of the nineteenth division of the temple musicians (26).
A priest who returned from Babylon ([Neh. 12:2](#Neh.12.2)).
A Levite of the family of Merari ([1 Chr. 6:44](#1Chr.6.44)).
An Amoritish chief in alliance with Abraham ([Gen. 14:13](#Gen.14.13), [24](#Gen.14.24)).

Consoler, a Christian teacher at Antioch. Nothing else is known of him beyond what is stated in [Acts 13:1](#Acts.13.1), where he is spoken of as having been brought up with (Gr. syntrophos; rendered in R.V. “foster brother” of) Herod, i.e., Herod Antipas, the tetrach, who, with his brother Archelaus, was educated at Rome.

The elder of the two sons of Joseph. He and his brother Ephraim were afterwards adopted by Jacob as his own sons (48:1). There is an account of his marriage to a Syrian ([1 Chr. 7:14](#1Chr.7.14)); and the only thing afterwards recorded of him is, that his grandchildren were “brought up upon Joseph’s knees” ([Gen. 50:23](#Gen.50.23); R.V., “born upon Joseph’s knees”) i.e., were from their birth adopted by Joseph as his own children.

The elder of the two sons of Joseph. He and his brother Ephraim were afterwards adopted by Jacob as his own sons (48:1). There is an account of his marriage to a Syrian ([1 Chr. 7:14](#1Chr.7.14)); and the only thing afterwards recorded of him is, that his grandchildren were “brought up upon Joseph’s knees” ([Gen. 50:23](#Gen.50.23); R.V., “born upon Joseph’s knees”) i.e., were from their birth adopted by Joseph as his own children.
Rest, a Danite, the father of Samson ([Judg. 13:1-22](#Judg.13.1), and 14:2-4).

Bitterness, the sister of Lazarus and Mary, and probably the eldest of the family, who all resided at Bethany ([Luke 10:38](#Luke.10.38), [40](#Luke.10.40), [41](#Luke.10.41); [John 11:1-39](#John.11.1)). From the residence being called “her house,” some have supposed that she was a widow, and that her brother and sister lodged with her. She seems to have been of an anxious, bustling spirit, anxious to be helpful in providing the best things for the Master’s use, in contrast to the quiet earnestness of Mary, who was more concerned to avail herself of the opportunity of sitting at his feet and learning of him. Afterwards at a supper given to Christ and his disciples in her house “Martha served.” Nothing further is known of her.

The wife of Joseph, the mother of Jesus, called the “Virgin Mary,” though never so designated in Scripture ([Matt. 2:11](#Matt.2.11); [Acts 1:14](#Acts.1.14)). Little is known of her personal history. Her genealogy is given in [Luke 3](#Luke.3). She was of the tribe of Judah and the lineage of David ([Ps. 132:11](#Ps.132.11); [Luke 1:32](#Luke.1.32)). She was connected by marriage with Elisabeth, who was of the lineage of Aaron ([Luke 1:36](#Luke.1.36)).

A surname derived from Magdala, the place of her nativity, given to one of the Marys of the Gospels to distinguish her from the other Marys ([Matt. 27:56](#Matt.27.56), [61](#Matt.27.61); 28:1, etc.). A mistaken notion has prevailed that this Mary was a woman of bad character, that she was the woman who is emphatically called “a sinner” ([Luke 7:36-50](#Luke.7.36)).
Mary the sister of Lazarus is brought to our notice in connection with the visits of our Lord to Bethany. …

Mary the mother of John Mark was one of the earliest of our Lord’s disciples. She was the sister of Barnabas ([Col. 4:10](#Col.4.10)), and joined with him in disposing of their land and giving the proceeds of the sale into the treasury of the Church ([Acts 4:37](#Acts.4.37); [12:12](#Acts.12.12)). Her house in Jerusalem was the common meeting-place for the disciples there.
A Christian at Rome who treated Paul with special kindness ([Rom. 16:6](#Rom.16.6)).

(= Meshech [1 Chr. 1:17](#1Chr.1.17)), one of the four sons of Aram, and the name of a tribe descended from him ([Gen. 10:23](#Gen.10.23)) inhabiting some part probably of Mesopotamia. Some have supposed that they were the inhabitants of Mount Masius, the present Karja Baghlar, which forms part of the chain of Taurus.
A lifting up, gift, one of the sons of Ishmael, the founder of an Arabian tribe ([Gen. 25:14](#Gen.25.14)); a nomad tribe inhabiting the Arabian desert toward Babylonia.
A priest of Baal, slain before his altar during the reformation under Jehoiada ([2 Kings 11:18](#2Kgs.11.18)).
A Levite, son of Heman, the chief of the ninth class of temple singers ([1 Chr. 25:4](#1Chr.25.4), [16](#1Chr.25.16)).
A Levite who assisted in purifying the temple at the reformation under Hezekiah ([2 Chr. 29:13](#2Chr.29.13)).
The son of Amos, in the genealogy of our Lord ([Luke 3:25](#Luke.3.25)).
The son of Semei, in the same genealogy ([Luke 3:26](#Luke.3.26)).
The son of Eleazar, and father of Jacob, who was the father of Joseph, the husband of the Virgin Mary ([Matt. 1:15](#Matt.1.15)).
The son of Levi, and father of Heli ([Luke 3:24](#Luke.3.24)).

Gift of God, a common Jewish name after the Exile. He was the son of Alphaeus, and was a publican or tax-gatherer at Capernaum. On one occasion Jesus, coming up from the side of the lake, passed the custom-house where Matthew was seated, and said to him, “Follow me.” Matthew arose and followed him, and became his disciple ([Matt. 9:9](#Matt.9.9)). Formerly the name by which he was known was Levi ([Mark 2:14](#Mark.2.14); [Luke 5:27](#Luke.5.27)); he now changed it, possibly in grateful memory of his call, to Matthew. …
One of the sons of Jeduthun ([1 Chr. 25:3](#1Chr.25.3), [21](#1Chr.25.21)).
The eldest son of Shallum, of the family of Korah ([1 Chr. 9:31](#1Chr.9.31)).
One who stood by Ezra while reading the law ([Neh. 8:4](#Neh.8.4)).
A son of Jokshan, Abraham’s son by Keturah ([1 Chr. 1:32](#1Chr.1.32)). His descendants settled on the Syrian borders about the territory of Edom. They probably led a pastoral life.
Whose benefactor is God, the father of Delaiah, and grandfather of Shemaiah, who joined Sanballat against Nehemiah ([Neh. 6:10](#Neh.6.10)).
Wife of Hadad, one of the kings of Edom ([Gen. 36:39](#Gen.36.39)).
Smitten by God, the son of Irad, and father of Methusael ([Gen. 4:18](#Gen.4.18)).
Faithful, one of the eunchs whom Ahasuerus (Xerxes) commanded to bring in Vashti ([Esther 1:10](#Esth.1.10)).

Habitations, ([2 Chr. 26:7](#2Chr.26.7); R.V. “Meunim,” Vulg. Ammonitae), a people against whom Uzziah waged a successful war. This word is in Hebrew the plural of Ma’on, and thus denotes the Maonites who inhabited the country on the eastern side of the Wady el-Arabah. They are again mentioned in [1 Chr. 4:41](#1Chr.4.41) (R.V.), in the reign of King Hezekiah, as a Hamite people, settled in the eastern end of the valley of Gedor, in the wilderness south of Palestine. In this passage the Authorized Version has “habitation,” erroneously following the translation of Luther.
The son of Addi, and father of Neri ([Luke 3:28](#Luke.3.28)).

King of righteousness, the king of Salem (q.v.). All we know of him is recorded in [Gen. 14:18-20](#Gen.14.18). He is subsequently mentioned only once in the Old Testament, in [Ps. 110:4](#Ps.110.4). The typical significance of his history is set forth in detail in the Epistle to the Hebrews, ch. 7. The apostle there points out the superiority of his priesthood to that of Aaron in these several respects, (1) Even Abraham paid him tithes; (2) he blessed Abraham; (3) he is the type of a Priest who lives for ever; (4) Levi, yet unborn, paid him tithes in the person of Abraham; (5) the permanence of his priesthood in Christ implied the abrogation of the Levitical system; (6) he was made priest not without an oath; and (7) his priesthood can neither be transmitted nor interrupted by death: “this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood.”
Fulness, the son of Menan and father of Eliakim, in the genealogy of our Lord ([Luke 3:31](#Luke.3.31)).
King, the second of Micah’s four sons ([1 Chr. 8:35](#1Chr.8.35)), and thus grandson of Mephibosheth.

Probably a Persian word meaning master of wine, i.e., chief butler; the title of an officer at the Babylonian court ([Dan. 1:11](#Dan.1.11), [16](#Dan.1.16)) who had charge of the diet of the Hebrew youths.
Dignified, one of the royal counsellors at the court of Ahasuerus, by whose suggestion Vashti was divorced ([Esther 1:14](#Esth.1.14), [16](#Esth.1.16), [21](#Esth.1.21)).

Conforting, the son of Gadi, and successor of Shallum, king of Israel, whom he slew. After a reign of about ten years (B.C. 771-760) he died, leaving the throne to his son Pekahiah. His reign was one of cruelty and oppression ([2 Kings 15:14-22](#2Kgs.15.14)). During his reign, Pul (q.v.), king of Assyria, came with a powerful force against Israel, but was induced to retire by a gift from Menahem of 1,000 talents of silver.

The son of Jonathan, and grandson of Saul ([2 Sam. 4:4](#2Sam.4.4)). He was but five years old when his father and grandfather fell on Mount Gilboa. The child’s nurse hearing of this calamity, fled with him from Gibeah, the royal residence, and stumbling in her haste, the child was thrown to the ground and maimed in both his feet, and ever after was unable to walk (19:26). He was carried to the land of Gilead, where he found a refuge in the house of Machir, the son of Ammiel, at Lo-debar, by whom he was brought up.

The name of Saul’s son by the concubine Rizpah (q.v.), the daughter of Aiah. He and his brother Armoni were with five others “hanged on a hill before the Lord” by the Gibeonites, and their bodies exposed in the sun for five months ([2 Sam. 21:8-10](#2Sam.21.8)).

Increase, the eldest of Saul’s two daughters ([1 Sam. 14:49](#1Sam.14.49)). She was betrothed to David after his victory over Goliath, but does not seem to have entered heartily into this arrangement (18:2, 17, 19). She was at length, however, married to Adriel of Abel-Meholah, a town in the Jordan valley, about 10 miles south of Bethshean, with whom the house of Saul maintained alliance. She had five sons, who were all put to death by the Gibeonites on the hill of Gibeah ([2 Sam. 21:8](#2Sam.21.8)).
Resistance, a chief priest, a contemporary of the high priest Joiakim ([Neh. 12:12](#Neh.12.12)).
Father of Amariah, a high priest of the line of Eleazar ([1 Chr. 6:6](#1Chr.6.6), [7](#1Chr.6.7), [52](#1Chr.6.52)).

Sad; bitter, the youngest son of Levi, born before the descent of Jacob into Egypt, and one of the seventy who accompanied him thither ([Gen. 46:11](#Gen.46.11); [Ex. 6:16](#Exod.6.16)). He became the head of one of the great divisions of the Levites ([Ex. 6:19](#Exod.6.19)).
Rebellion, one of the sons of Ezra, of the tribe of Judah ([1 Chr. 4:17](#1Chr.4.17)).

Exaltations, heights, a priest who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel ([Neh. 12:3](#Neh.12.3)), to whom were sent the sacred vessels ([Ezra 8:33](#Ezra.8.33)) belonging to the temple. He took part in rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem ([Neh. 3:4](#Neh.3.4)).

Merodach has given a son, ([Isa. 39:1](#Isa.39.1)), “the hereditary chief of the Chaldeans, a small tribe at that time settled in the marshes at the mouth of the Euphrates, but in consequence of his conquest of Babylon afterwards, they became the dominant caste in Babylonia itself.” One bearing this name sent ambassadors to Hezekiah (B.C. 721). He is also called Berodach-baladan ([2 Kings 20:12](#2Kgs.20.12); [2 Chr. 20:31](#2Chr.20.31)).

Heb. id, a king of Moab, the son of Chemosh-Gad, a man of great wealth in flocks and herds ([2 Kings 3:4](#2Kgs.3.4)). After the death of Ahab at Ramoth-Gilead, Mesha shook off the yoke of Israel; but on the ascension of Jehoram to the throne of Israel, that king sought the help of Jehoshaphat in an attempt to reduce the Moabites again to their former condition. The united armies of the two kings came unexpectedly on the army of the Moabites, and gained over them an easy victory. …
Heb. meysh’a, “deliverance,” the eldest son of Caleb ([1 Chr. 2:42](#1Chr.2.42)), and brother of Jerahmeel.

One of the three Hebrew youths who were trained with Daniel in Babylon ([Dan. 1:11](#Dan.1.11), [19](#Dan.1.19)), and promoted to the rank of Magi. He and his companions were afterwards cast into the burning fiery furnace for refusing to worship the idol the king had set up, from which they were miraculously delivered (3:13-30). His Chaldean name was Meshach (q.v.).

Drawing out, the sixth son of Japheth ([Gen. 10:2](#Gen.10.2)), the founder of a tribe ([1 Chr. 1:5](#1Chr.1.5); [Ezek. 27:13](#Ezek.27.13); [38:2](#Ezek.38.2), [3](#Ezek.38.3)). They were in all probability the Moschi, a people inhabiting the Moschian Mountains, between the Black and the Caspian Seas. In [Ps. 120:5](#Ps.120.5) the name occurs as simply a synonym for foreigners or barbarians. “During the ascendency of the Babylonians and Persians in Western Asia, the Moschi were subdued; but it seems probable that a large number of them crossed the Caucasus range and spread over the northern steppes, mingling with the Scythians. There they became known as Muscovs, and gave that name to the Russian nation and its ancient capital by which they are still generally known throughout the East”

Friendship of Jehovah, a Levite of the family of the Korhites, called also Shelemiah ([1 Chr. 9:21](#1Chr.9.21); [26:1](#1Chr.26.1), [2](#1Chr.26.2), [9](#1Chr.26.9), [14](#1Chr.26.14)). He was a temple gate-keeper in the time of David.
A priest, the son of Immer ([Neh. 11:13](#Neh.11.13)).
Grandfather of Shaphan, “the scribe,” in the reign of Josiah ([2 Kings 22:3](#2Kgs.22.3)).
One of the chief Gadites in Bashan in the time of Jotham ([1 Chr. 5:13](#1Chr.5.13)).
One of the principal Israelites who supported Ezra when expounding the law to the people ([Neh. 8:4](#Neh.8.4)).
Friend, the wife of Manasseh, and the mother of Amon ([2 Kings 21:19](#2Kgs.21.19)), Kings of Judah.
Champion of El; man of God, a descendant of Cain ([Gen. 4:18](#Gen.4.18)), so called, perhaps, to denote that even among the descendants of Cain God had not left himself without a witness.

Man of the dart, the son of Enoch, and grandfather of Noah. He was the oldest man of whom we have any record, dying at the age of nine hundred and sixty-nine years, in the year of the Flood ([Gen. 5:21-27](#Gen.5.21); [1 Chr. 1:3](#1Chr.1.3)).
Water of gold, the father of Matred ([Gen. 36:39](#Gen.36.39); [1 Chr. 1:50](#1Chr.1.50)), and grandfather of Mehetabel, wife of Hadar, the last king of Edom.
Choice, a Hagarene, one of David’s warriors ([1 Chr. 11:38](#1Chr.11.38)); called also Bani the Gadite ([2 Sam. 23:36](#2Sam.23.36)).
One of Ishmael’s twelve sons, and head of an Arab tribe ([Gen. 25:13](#Gen.25.13)).
Fortress, one of the Edomitish “dukes” descended from Esau ([Gen. 36:42](#Gen.36.42); [1 Chr. 1:53](#1Chr.1.53)).

A man of Mount Ephraim, whose history so far is introduced in [Judg. 17](#Judg.17), apparently for the purpose of leading to an account of the settlement of the tribe of Dan in Northern Palestine, and for the purpose also of illustrating the lawlessness of the times in which he lived ([Judg. 18](#Judg.18); [19:1-29](#Judg.19.1); [21:25](#Judg.21.25)).

“The Morasthite,” so called to distinguish him from Micaiah, the son of Imlah ([1 Kings 22:8](#1Kgs.22.8)). He was a prophet of Judah, a contemporary of Isaiah ([Micah 1:1](#Mic.1.1)), a native of Moresheth of Gath (1:14, 15). Very little is known of the circumstances of his life (comp. [Jer. 26:18](#Jer.26.18), [19](#Jer.26.19)).
A descendant of Joel the Reubenite ([1 Chr. 5:5](#1Chr.5.5)).

Who is like Jehovah?, the son of Imlah, a faithful prophet of Samaria ([1 Kings 22:8-28](#1Kgs.22.8)). Three years after the great battle with Ben-hadad (20:29-34), Ahab proposed to Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, that they should go up against Ramoth-Gilead to do battle again with Ben-hadad. Jehoshaphat agreed, but suggested that inquiry should be first made “at the word of Jehovah.” Ahab’s prophets approved of the expedition; but Jehoshaphat, still dissatisfied, asked if there was no other prophet besides the four hundred that had appeared, and was informed of this Micaiah. …
The son of Zabdi, a Levite of the family of Asaph ([Neh. 11:17](#Neh.11.17), [22](#Neh.11.22)).

The title given to one of the chief angels ([Dan. 10:13](#Dan.10.13), [21](#Dan.10.21); 12:1). He had special charge of Israel as a nation. He disputed with Satan ([Jude 1](#Jude.1.1):9) about the body of Moses. He is also represented as warning against “that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world” ([Rev. 12:7-9](#Rev.12.7)).
The father of Sethur, the spy selected to represent Asher ([Num. 13:13](#Num.13.13)).
A chief Gadite in Bashan ([1 Chr. 5:13](#1Chr.5.13)).
[1 Chr. 7:3](#1Chr.7.3), a chief of the tribe of Issachar.
A Manassite, “a captain of thousands” who joined David at Ziklag ([1 Chr. 12:20](#1Chr.12.20)).
